title: Force another program's standard output to be unbuffered using Python
question: Force another program's standard output to be unbuffered using Python A python script is controlling an external application on Linux, passing in input via a pipe to the external applications stdin, and reading output via a pipe from the external applications stdout. The problem is that writes to pipes are buffered by block, and not by line, and therefore delays occur before the controlling script receives data output by, for example, printf in the external application. The external application cannot be altered to add explicit fflush(0) calls. How can the pty module of the python standard library be used with the subprocess module to achieve this?
answer: Doing this is possible, but the only solution I can think of is fairly convoluted, non-portable, and probably fraught with problematic details.  You can use LD_PRELOAD to cause the external application to load a dynamic library which contains a constructor that invokes setvbuf to unbuffer stdout.  You will probably also want to wrap setvbuf in the library to prevent the application from explicitly buffering its own stdout.  And you'll want to wrap fwrite and printf so that they flush on each call.  Writing the .so to be preloaded will take you outside of python.

title: Error handling when importing modules
question: Error handling when importing modules This probably has an obvious answer, but I'm a beginner.  I've got a "module" (really just a file with a bunch of functions I often use) at the beginning of which I import a number of other modules.  Because I work on many systems, however, not all modules may be able to load on any particular machine.  To make things slightly more difficult, I also change the names of the packages when I import them -- for example, matplotlib gets abbreviated to mp. What I'd like to do is only load those modules that exist on the system I'm currently using, and do some error handling on the ones that don't.  The only way I can think of doing so is by enclosing each import statement inside its own try block, which seems pretty un-pythonic.  If I enclose them all in the same try block, whichever module throws an error will prevent the subsequent modules from being loaded.  Any ideas that might make things look prettier?  It would be so easy if I didn't want to change their names... Thanks! Dave
answer:
I don't think [CODE] try except [/CODE] block is un-pythonic; instead it's a common way to handle import on Python. Quoting Dive into Python : There are a lot of other uses for
  exceptions besides handling actual
  error conditions. A common use in the
  standard Python library is to try to
  import a module, and then check
  whether it worked . Importing a module
  that does not exist will raise an
  ImportError exception. You can use
  this to define multiple levels of
  functionality based on which modules
  are available at run-time, or to
  support multiple platforms (where
  platform-specific code is separated
  into different modules). The next example demonstrates how to
  use an exception to support
  platform-specific functionality. [CODE] try:
    import termios, TERMIOS                     
except ImportError:
    try:
        import msvcrt                           
    except ImportError:
        try:
            from EasyDialogs import AskPassword 
        except ImportError:
            getpass = default_getpass           
        else:                                   
            getpass = AskPassword
    else:
        getpass = win_getpass
else:
    getpass = unix_getpass
 [/CODE]

title: What happen to a list when passed to a function?
question:
What happen to a list when passed to a function? I'm trying to understand how a list is treated when passed as an argument to a function. So what I did was the following: I initialized a list: [CODE] ll = [1,2,3,4] 
 [/CODE] and define a function: [CODE] def Foo(ar):
    ar += [11]
 [/CODE] I passed the list to the function: [CODE] Foo(ll)
 [/CODE] and when I print it I got: [CODE] print ll # [1, 2, 3, 4, 11] #case(1)
 [/CODE] So far so good. Now I modified the function in order to reset the list such that it has a single element only: [CODE] def Foo(ar):
    ar = [11]
 [/CODE] I recalled the syntax: [CODE] Foo(ll)
 [/CODE] and when I reprint it, it resulted in the same list: [CODE] print ll # [1, 2, 3, 4] # case(2)
 [/CODE] I thought the list was passed as reference; so whatever we do to the list inside a function will always change the original function passed from the main program. So for case(2) I was expecting the following result: [CODE] print ll # [11] # case(2) expected result
 [/CODE] Am I missing something here?
answer:
[CODE] ar += [11] [/CODE] is not just an assignment. It's a method call (the method called is: [CODE] __iadd__ [/CODE] ). when Python executes that line it calls the method and then assigns [CODE] ar [/CODE] to the result. The [CODE] __iadd__ [/CODE] method of [CODE] list [/CODE] modifies the current [CODE] list [/CODE] . [CODE] ar = [11] [/CODE] is an assignment and hence it simply changes the value of the local name [CODE] ar [/CODE] . But there is no link between the [CODE] ar [/CODE] name inside the function and the value of the [CODE] ll [/CODE] variable. You probably want something like: [CODE] ar[:] = [11]
 [/CODE]

title: Check if file has a CSV format with Python
question: Check if file has a CSV format with Python Could someone provide an effective way to check if a file has CSV format using Python ?
answer:
You could try something like the following, but just because you get a dialect back from [CODE] csv.Sniffer [/CODE] really won't be sufficient for guaranteeing you have a valid CSV document. [CODE] csv_fileh = open(somefile, 'rb')
try:
    dialect = csv.Sniffer().sniff(csv_fileh.read(1024))
    # Perform various checks on the dialect (e.g., lineseparator,
    # delimiter) to make sure it's sane

    # Don't forget to reset the read position back to the start of
    # the file before reading any entries.
    csv_fileh.seek(0)
except csv.Error:
    # File appears not to be in CSV format; move along
 [/CODE]

title: Get date from week number
question:
Get date from week number Please what's wrong with my code: [CODE] import datetime
d = "2013-W26"
r = datetime.datetime.strptime(d, "%Y-W%W")
print(r)
 [/CODE] Display "2013-01-01 00:00:00", Thanks.
answer:
A week number is not enough to generate a date; you need a day of the week as well. Add a default: [CODE] import datetime
d = "2013-W26"
r = datetime.datetime.strptime(d + '-0', "%Y-W%W-%w")
print(r)
 [/CODE] The [CODE] -0 [/CODE] and [CODE] -%w [/CODE] pattern tells the parser to pick the sunday in that week. This outputs: [CODE] 2013-07-07 00:00:00
 [/CODE] You can pick your own weekday, whatever fits your use case best; the [CODE] %W [/CODE] pattern bases weeks from monday, so perhaps [CODE] -1 [/CODE] is a better default here. See the [CODE] strftime() [/CODE] and [CODE] strptime() [/CODE] behaviour section in the documentation, footnote 4: When used with the [CODE] strptime() [/CODE] method, [CODE] %U [/CODE] and [CODE] %W [/CODE] are only used in calculations when the day of the week and the year are specified.

title: Sklearn.KMeans() : Get class centroid labels and reference to a dataset
question:
Sklearn.KMeans() : Get class centroid labels and reference to a dataset Sci-Kit learn Kmeans and PCA dimensionality reduction I have a dataset, 2M rows by 7 columns, with different measurements of home power consumption with a date for each measurement. date, Global_active_power, Global_reactive_power, Voltage, Global_intensity, Sub_metering_1, Sub_metering_2, Sub_metering_3 I put my dataset into a pandas dataframe, selecting all columns but the date column, then perform cross validation split. [CODE] import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cross_validation import train_test_split

data = pd.read_csv('household_power_consumption.txt', delimiter=';')
power_consumption = data.iloc[0:, 2:9].dropna()
pc_toarray = power_consumption.values
hpc_fit, hpc_fit1 = train_test_split(pc_toarray, train_size=.01)
power_consumption.head()
 [/CODE] I use K-means classification followed by PCA dimensionality reduction to display. [CODE] from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

hpc = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(hpc_fit)
k_means = KMeans()
k_means.fit(hpc)

x_min, x_max = hpc[:, 0].min() - 5, hpc[:, 0].max() - 1
y_min, y_max = hpc[:, 1].min(), hpc[:, 1].max() + 5
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, .02), np.arange(y_min, y_max, .02))
Z = k_means.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)

plt.figure(1)
plt.clf()
plt.imshow(Z, interpolation='nearest',
          extent=(xx.min(), xx.max(), yy.min(), yy.max()),
          cmap=plt.cm.Paired,
          aspect='auto', origin='lower')

plt.plot(hpc[:, 0], hpc[:, 1], 'k.', markersize=4)
centroids = k_means.cluster_centers_
inert = k_means.inertia_
plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1],
           marker='x', s=169, linewidths=3,
           color='w', zorder=8)
plt.xlim(x_min, x_max)
plt.ylim(y_min, y_max)
plt.xticks(())
plt.yticks(())
plt.show()
 [/CODE] Now I would like to find out which rows fell under a given class then whic
answer:
KMeans().predict(X) ..docs here Predict the closest cluster each sample in X belongs to. In the vector quantization literature, cluster_centers_ is called the code book and each value returned by predict is the index of the closest code in the code book. [CODE] Parameters: (New data to predict)

X : {array-like, sparse matrix}, shape = [n_samples, n_features]

Returns: (Index of the cluster each sample belongs to)  

labels : array, shape [n_samples,]
 [/CODE] The problem I with the code you submitted is the use of [CODE] train_test_split()
 [/CODE] which returns two arrays of random rows in your data-set, effectively ruining your dataset order making it difficult to correlate the labels returned from KMeans classification to sequential dates in your data set. Here's an example: [CODE] import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

#read data into pandas dataframe
df = pd.read_csv('household_power_consumption.txt', delimiter=';')
 [/CODE] [CODE] #convert merge date and time colums and convert to datetime objects
df['Datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Date'] + ' ' + df['Time'])
df.set_index(pd.DatetimeIndex(df['Datetime'],inplace=True))
df.drop(['Date','Time'], axis=1, inplace=True)

#put last column first
cols = df.columns.tolist()
cols = cols[-1:] + cols[:-1]
df = df[cols]
df = df.dropna()
 [/CODE] [CODE] #convert dataframe to data array and removes date column not to be processed, 
sliced = df.iloc[0:, 1:8].dropna()
hpc = sliced.values

k_means = KMeans()
k_means.fit(hpc)

# array of indexes corresponding to classes around centroids, in the order of your dataset
classified_data = k_means.labels_

#copy dataframe (may be memory intensive but just for illustration)
df_processed = df.copy()
df_processed['Cluster Class'] = pd.Series(classified_data, index=df_processed.index)
 [/CODE] Now you can see your result matched with your data-set on the right side. Now that it's classified, it's up to you to derive meaning. This is just a good overall example of how it can be used, from start to finish. Displaying your result, look at PCA or making other graphs dependent on class.

title: How to efficiently remove the same-length elements from a list in python
question: How to efficiently remove the same-length elements from a list in python For example, I have a list: [CODE] [[1,3],[23,4],[13,45,6],[8,3],[44,33,12]] [/CODE] Is there any efficient way that I can finally get the list below? [CODE] [[1,3],[13,45,6]] [/CODE] For every length of the list, keep only one element.
answer:
Just make a dictionary keyed off the length and get its values: [CODE] >>> l = [[1,3],[23,4],[13,45,6],[8,3],[44,33,12]]
>>> dict((len(i), i) for i in l).values()
[[8, 3], [44, 33, 12]]
 [/CODE]

title: How to chose an AWS profile when using boto3 to connect to CloudFront
question:
How to chose an AWS profile when using boto3 to connect to CloudFront I am using the Boto 3 python library, and want to connect to AWS CloudFront.
I need to specify the correct AWS Profile (AWS Credentials), but looking at the official documentation, I see no way to specify it. I am initializing the client using the code: [CODE] client = boto3.client('cloudfront') [/CODE] However, this results in it using the default profile to connect.
I couldn't find a method where I can specify which profile to use.
answer:
I think the docs aren't wonderful at exposing how to do this. It has been a supported feature for some time, however, and there are some details in this pull request . So there are three ways to do this: Create a new session with the profile [CODE] dev = boto3.session.Session(profile_name='dev')
 [/CODE] Change the profile of the default session in code [CODE] boto3.setup_default_session(profile_name='dev')
 [/CODE] Change the profile of the default session with an environment variable [CODE] $ AWS_PROFILE=dev ipython
>>> import boto3
>>> s3dev = boto3.resource('s3')
 [/CODE]

title: Linestyle in matplotlib step function
question:
Linestyle in matplotlib step function Is it possible to set the linestyle in a matplotlib step function to dashed, dotted, etc.? I've tried: [CODE] step(x, linestyle='--'), 
step(x, '--')
 [/CODE] But it did not help.
answer:
As of mpl 1.3.0 this is fixed upstream You have to come at it a bit sideways as [CODE] step [/CODE] seems to ignore [CODE] linestyle [/CODE] .  If you look at what [CODE] step [/CODE] is doing underneath, it is just a thin wrapper for plot. You can do what you want by talking to [CODE] plot [/CODE] directly: [CODE] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(range(5), range(5), linestyle='--', drawstyle='steps')
plt.plot(range(5), range(5)[::-1], linestyle=':', drawstyle='steps')
plt.xlim([-1, 5])
plt.ylim([-1, 5])
 [/CODE] [CODE] ['steps', 'steps-pre', 'steps-mid', 'steps-post'] [/CODE] are the valid values for [CODE] drawstyle [/CODE] and  control where the step is drawn. Pull request resulting from this question, I personally think this is a bug. [edit: this has been pulled into master and should show up in v1.3.0].

title: Pickling inner classes
answer: When an inner class is created, there is no way for the interpreter to know which class it was defined inside of, this information is not recorded. This is why pickle does not know where to look for the class Article. Because of this there are numerous issues when using inner classes, not just when it comes to pickling. If there are classes at the module scope with the same name, it introduces a lot of ambiguity as there is no easy way to tell the two types apart (e.g. with repr or when debugging.) As a result it is generally best to avoid nested classes in Python unless you have a very good reason for doing so.

title: How to remove whitespace in BeautifulSoup
question:
How to remove whitespace in BeautifulSoup I have a bunch of HTML I'm parsing with BeautifulSoup and it's been going pretty well except for one minor snag. I want to save the output into a single-lined string, with the following as my current output: [CODE]
  • Zazzafooky but one two three!
  • Zazzafooky2
  • Zazzafooky3
    • [/CODE] Ideally I'd like [CODE]
  • Zazzafooky but one two three!
  • Zazzafooky2
    • [/CODE] There's a lot of redundant whitespace that I'd like to get rid of but it's not necessarily removable using [CODE] strip() [/CODE] , nor can I blatantly remove all the spaces because I need to retain the text. How can I do it? It seems like a common enough problem that regex would be overkill, but is that the only way? I don't have any [CODE] 
     [/CODE] tags so I can be a little more forceful there. Thanks once again!
answer:
Here is how you can do it without regular expressions: [CODE] >>> html = """
  • ... Zazzafooky but one two three! ...
    • ...
  • ... Zazzafooky2 ...
    • ...
  • ... Zazzafooky3 ...
    • ... """ >>> html = "".join(line.strip() for line in html.split("\n")) >>> html '
  • Zazzafooky but one two three!
  • Zazzafooky2
  • Zazzafooky3
    • ' [/CODE]

index = date_range(time_start[0],time_end[0],freq='30S')

 [/CODE] Here the first column is the index and second column is the value. My task is to collect all moments that their values (second column) are missing. What I thought is this way: [CODE] for i in s:

      s.iloc['i']

title: Is there a way to store python objects directly in mongoDB without serializing them
question: Is there a way to store python objects directly in mongoDB without serializing them I have read somewhere that you can store python objects (more specifically dictionaries) as binaries in MongoDB by using BSON. However right now I cannot find any any documentation related to this. Would anyone know how exactly this can be done?
answer:
There isn't a way to store an object in a file (database) without serializing it. If the data needs to move from one process to another process or to another server, it will need to be serialized in some form to be transmitted. Since you're asking about MongoDB, the data will absolutely be serialized in some form in order to be stored in the MongoDB database. When using MongoDB, it's BSON . If you're actually asking about whether there would be a way to store a more raw form of a Python object in a MongoDB document, you can insert a [CODE] Binary [/CODE] field into a document which can contain any data you'd like. It's not directly queryable in any way in that form, so you're potentially loosing a lot of the benefits of using a NoSQL document database like MongoDB. [CODE] >>> from pymongo import MongoClient
>>> client = MongoClient('localhost', 27017)
>>> db = client['test-database']
>>> coll = db.test_collection    
>>> # the collection is ready now 
>>> from bson.binary import Binary
>>> import pickle
>>> # create a sample object
>>> myObj = {}
>>> myObj['demo'] = 'Some demo data'
>>> # convert it to the raw bytes
>>> thebytes = pickle.dump(myObj)
>>> coll.insert({'bin-data': Binary(thebytes)})
 [/CODE]

title: How to prevent my site page to be loaded via 3rd party site frame of iFrame
question: How to prevent my site page to be loaded via 3rd party site frame of iFrame How can I find out that my page is embedded as a frame to other site during page loading? I guess referrer request header can't help me here? Thanks.
answer: You cannot check it from the server's side, but you can use javascript to detect it after the page has loaded. Compare [CODE] top [/CODE] and [CODE] self [/CODE] , if they're not identical, you are in a frame. Additionally, some modern browsers respect the [CODE] X-FRAME-OPTIONS [/CODE] header, that can have two values: DENY â prevents the page from being rendered if it is contained in a frame SAMEORIGIN â same as above, unless the page belongs to the same domain as the top-level frameset holder. Users include Google's Picasa, that cannot be embedded in a frame. Browsers that support the header, with the minimum version: IE8 and IE9 Opera 10.50 Safari 4 Chrome 4.1.249.1042 Firefox 3.6.9 (older versions with NoScript )

question:
Fix first element, shuffle the rest of a list/array Is it possible to shuffle only a (continuous) part of a given list (or array in numpy)? If this is not generally possible, how about the special case where the first element is fixed while the rest of the list/array need to be shuffled? For example, I have a list/array: [CODE] to_be_shuffled = [None, 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', ...]
 [/CODE] where the first element should always stay, while the rest are going to be shuffled repeatedly. One possible way is to shuffle the whole list first, and then check the first element, if it is not the special fixed element (e.g. [CODE] None [/CODE] ), then swap its position with that of the special element (which would then require a lookup). Is there any better way for doing this?
answer:
Why not just [CODE] import random
rest = to_be_shuffled[1:]
random.shuffle(rest)
shuffled_lst = [to_be_shuffled[0]] + rest
 [/CODE]

title: Django datefield and timefield to python datetime
question:
Django datefield and timefield to python datetime I have a Django model with separate Datefield and Timefield for an event. Is there a way to convert it to a python datetime object so I can query for the upcoming events with some precision? Currently I get only the upcoming of the following day. models.py [CODE] event_time = models.TimeField()
event_date = models.DateField()
 [/CODE] Basically, can I filter with a minute, or even split second precition? Thank you.
answer:
Use a [CODE] DateTimeField [/CODE] instead (see this section in the docs). Conversion to a [CODE] datetime.datetime [/CODE] is handled for you by Django automatically. A [CODE] DateField [/CODE] results in a [CODE] datetime.date [/CODE] and a [CODE] datetime.time [/CODE] object. You can use [CODE] replace [/CODE] to merge these values into an updated [CODE] date [/CODE] : >>> today = datetime.datetime.today()
>>> today
datetime.datetime(2012, 3, 31, 11, 6, 5, 182371)
>>> time = datetime.time(11, 30)
>>> today.replace(hour=time.hour, minute=time.minute)
datetime.datetime(2012, 3, 31, 11, 30, 5, 182371) Note that the resulting [CODE] date [/CODE] has 11.30 as time now. Note also that [CODE] today [/CODE] is not modified, it simply computes a new date and time. As you can see, you now have to do the merging yourself because both values are stored in separate fields. That's why a [CODE] DateTimeField [/CODE] is a much better choice, if you have the ability to modify the model's fields.

title: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append'
question:
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' I have a weird problem with python passing a list as parameter to a function. Here is the code: [CODE] def foobar(depth, top, bottom, n=len(listTop)):
    print dir(top)
    print top.append("hi")
    if depth > 0:
        exit()
    foobar(depth+1, top.append(listTop[i]), bottom.append(listBottom[i]))

top = bottom = []
foobar(0, top, bottom)
 [/CODE] It says "AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append'", because top is None in foobar although dir(top) prints a full attribute and method list of a type list.
So whats wrong? I just wanted to pass two lists as parameters to this recursive function.
answer:
You pass in the result of [CODE] top.append() [/CODE] to your function. [CODE] top.append() [/CODE] returns None: [CODE] >>> [].append(0) is None
True
 [/CODE] You need to call [CODE] .append() [/CODE] separately, then pass in just [CODE] top [/CODE] : [CODE] top.append(listTop[i])
bottom.append(listBottom[i])
foobar(depth+1, top, bottom)
 [/CODE] Note that the [CODE] n=len(listTop) [/CODE] argument in the function is both redundant and only ever executed once, namely when you create the function. It won't be evaluated each time you call the function. You can omit it safely from the version you posted here in any case.

question:
PyCharm noinspection for whole file? Is it possible to disable an inspection for the whole file in PyCharm? The reason this is needed is when dealing with py.test . It uses fixtures which appear to shadow function parameters, and at the same time cause unresolved references. e.g.: [CODE] from myfixtures import user  # Unused import statement warning

def test_is_awesome(user):  # Shadows name 'user' from outer scope warning
    assert user.is_awesome()
 [/CODE] There is also other warnings from py.test, such as using [CODE] pytest.raises() [/CODE] causes a "Can not find reference 'raises'" in pytest.py. Maybe there's another way to fix these problems? Maybe I'm using py.test incorrectly?
answer: Is it possible to disable an inspection for the whole file in PyCharm? Yes. This answer is for this question only (and not about "Maybe there's another way to fix these problems? Maybe I'm using py.test incorrectly?" ). "Settings | Scopes" Create new scope that would include such "unwanted" file(s) "Settings | Inspections" Find "problematic" inspection Right click and choose "Add scope" Disable that inspection for that specific scope Alternatively (may work or may not: depends on actual inspection .. and I'm not sure if it actually works in PyCharm this way -- not a PyCharm user myself unfortunately) Alt + Enter while caret is standing on error/warning place in your code Select correct entry from appeared popup menu Using Arrow Right key expand submenu Look for "Suppress inspection" option This is how it looks in PhpStorm (screenshot shows "suppress for statement" option and not "suppress for whole file"): Related: http://stackoverflow.com/a/20803118/783119

Question: replace() function is not replacing 'e' character

replace() function is not replacing 'e' character My code should recognize the vowel letters and remove them from input string using the [CODE] replace() [/CODE] function. However it works fine except for the [CODE] 'e' [/CODE] letter. If the input is [CODE] "Hey look Words!" [/CODE] the output is [CODE] "Hey lk Wrds!" [/CODE] .
It identifies the 'e' only if if the "vowels" string is equal to [CODE] "e" [/CODE] or [CODE] "eE" [/CODE] only! I am curious to know why? [CODE] def anti_vowel(text):
vowles="AaEeOoIiUu"
newstr=""
for i in text:
    if i in vowles:
        newstr=text.replace(i,"")

return newstr
 [/CODE]

Answer: You are placing only the last replacement result in [CODE] newstr [/CODE] . All your previous [CODE] str.replace() [/CODE] results are discarded. For your input text [CODE] Hey look Words! [/CODE] , the last vowel encountered is [CODE] o [/CODE] so only [CODE] o [/CODE] is replaced. The [CODE] e [/CODE] replacement did take place and was stored in [CODE] newstr [/CODE] but that value was then discarded when you set [CODE] newstr [/CODE] to the result of the [CODE] o [/CODE] replacement. It thus depends on the input string what vowel exactly will remain replaced; for the sentence [CODE] 'The cat sat on the mat' [/CODE] it'll be [CODE] a [/CODE] as that is the last vowel you test and replace. Just loop directly over [CODE] vowels [/CODE] and replace each of those characters; it is save to call [CODE] str.replace() [/CODE] where the first argument is not present. Store the result back in [CODE] text [/CODE] so that any subsequent replacements stick: [CODE] def anti_vowel(text):
    vowels = "AaEeOoIiUu"
    for vowel in vowels:
        text = text.replace(vowel, "")
    return text
 [/CODE] Better still, use the [CODE] str.translate() [/CODE] method to replace all vowels in one go: [CODE] # Python 2 version
def anti_vowel(text):
    vowels = "AaEeOoIiUu"
    return text.translate(None, vowels)

# Python 3 version
def anti_vowel(text):
    vowels = str.maketrans(dict.fromkeys("AaEeOoIiUu"))
    return text.translate(vowels)
 [/CODE] [CODE] str.translate() [/CODE] makes all replacements at once; the method changed between Python 2 [CODE] str [/CODE] and Python 3 [CODE] str [/CODE] , but in both versions all the vowels are ignored as the new string is built, without any further loops.

title: How do I remove hex values in a python string with regular expressions?
question:
How do I remove hex values in a python string with regular expressions? I have a cell array in matlab [CODE] columns = {'MagX', 'MagY', 'MagZ', ...
           'AccelerationX',  'AccelerationX',  'AccelerationX', ...
           'AngularRateX', 'AngularRateX', 'AngularRateX', ...
           'Temperature'}
 [/CODE] I use these scripts which make use of matlab's hdf5write function to save the array in the hdf5 format. I then read in the the hdf5 file into python using pytables. The cell array comes in as a numpy array of strings. I convert to a list and this is the output: [CODE] >>>columns
['MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f',
 'MagY\x00\x7f\x00\x00\x00\xee\x0b9\xe6\x7f',
 'MagZ\x00\x00\x00\x00\x001',
 'AccelerationX',
 'AccelerationY',
 'AccelerationZ',
 'AngularRateX',
 'AngularRateY',
 'AngularRateZ',
 'Temperature']
 [/CODE] These hex values pop into the strings from somewhere and I'd like to remove them. They don't always appear on the first three items of the list and I need a nice way to deal with them or to find out why they are there in the first place. [CODE] >>>print columns[0]
Mag8ï¿½
>>>columns[0]
'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f'
>>>repr(columns[0])
"'MagX\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x08\\x01\\x008\\xe6\\x7f'"
>>>print repr(columns[0])
'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f'
 [/CODE] I've tried using a regular expression to remove the hex values but have little luck. [CODE] >>>re.sub('(\w*)\\\\x.*', '\1', columns[0])
'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f'
>>>re.sub('(\w*)\\\\x.*', r'\1', columns[0])
'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f'
>>>re.sub(r'(\w*)\\x.*', '\1', columns[0])
'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f'
>>>re.sub('([A-Za-z]*)\x00', r'\1', columns[0])
'MagX\x08\x018\xe6\x7f'
>>>re.sub('(\w*?)', '\1', columns[0])
'\x01M\x01a\x01g\x01X\x01\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00\x01\x08\x01\x01\x01\x00\x018\x01\xe6\x01\x7f\x01'
 [/CODE] Any suggestions on how to deal with this?
answer:
You can remove all non-word characters in the following way: [CODE] >>> re.sub(r'[^\w]', '', 'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f')
'MagX8'
 [/CODE] The regex [CODE] [^\w] [/CODE] will match any character that is not a letter, digit, or underscore.  By providing that regex in [CODE] re.sub [/CODE] with an empty string as a replacement you will delete all other characters in the string. Since there may be other characters you want to keep, a better solution might be to specify a larger range of characters that you want to keep that excludes control characters.  For example: [CODE] >>> re.sub(r'[^\x20-\x7e]', '', 'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f')
'MagX8'
 [/CODE] Or you could replace [CODE] [^\x20-\x7e] [/CODE] with the equivalent [CODE] [^ -~] [/CODE] , depending on which seems more clear to you. To exclude all characters after this first control character just add a [CODE] .* [/CODE] , like this: [CODE] >>> re.sub(r'[^ -~].*', '', 'MagX\x00\x00\x00\x08\x01\x008\xe6\x7f')
'MagX'
 [/CODE]

title: Finding zero values with odeint
question:
Finding zero values with odeint How can I find the point where the first derivative of my equation equals 0 using scipy.integrate.ode? I set up this function, which gets the answer, but I'm not sure about accuracy and it can't be the most efficient way to do this. Basically I am using this function to find the time a projectile with initial velocity stops moving. With systems of ODEs, is there a better way to solve for this answer? [CODE] import numpy as np
from scipy import integrate

def find_nearest(array,value):
    idx=(np.abs(array-value)).argmin()
    return array[idx], idx

def deriv(x,t):
    # This function sets up the following relations
    # dx/dt = v , dv/dt = -(Cp/m)*(4+v^2)
    return np.array([ x[1], -(0.005/0.1) * (4+ (x[1]**2)) ])

def findzero(start, stop, v0):
    time = np.linspace(start, stop, 100000)
    #xinit are initial vaules of equation
    xinit = np.array([0.0,v0]) 
    x = integrate.odeint(deriv,xinit,time)
    # find nearest velocity value nearest to 0
    value, num = find_nearest(x[:,1],0.0001)
    print 'closest value ',
    print value
    print 'reaches zero at time ',
    print time[num]
    return time[num]
# from 0 to 20 seconds with initial velocity of 100 m/s
b = findzero(0.0,20.0,100.0)
 [/CODE]
answer: In general, a good approach to solve this sort of problem is to rewrite your equations so that velocity is the independent variable and time and distance are the dependent variables. Then, you simply have to integrate the equations from v=v0 to v=0. However, in the example you give it is not even necessary to resort to [CODE] scipy.integrate [/CODE] at all. The equations can be easily solved with pencil and paper (separation of variables followed by a standard integral). The result is t = (m/(2 Cp)) arctan(v0/2) where v0 is the initial velocity and the result of arctan must be taken in radians. For an initial velocity of 100 m/s, the answer is 15.5079899282 seconds.

The equations can be easily solved with pencil and paper (separation of variables followed by a standard integral). The result is t = (m/(2 Cp)) arctan(v0/2) where v0 is the initial velocity and the result of arctan must be taken in radians. For an initial velocity of 100 m/s, the answer is 15.5079899282 seconds.

title: Python: String formatting a regex string that uses both '%' and '{' as characters
question:
Python: String formatting a regex string that uses both '%' and '{' as characters I have the following regular expression, which lets me parse percentages like '20%+', '20%', or '20% - 50%' using re.split. [CODE] '([0-9]{1,3}[%])([+-]?)'
 [/CODE] I want to use string formatting to pass the series identifiers (i.e. '+-') as an argument from config.py. [CODE] SERIES = '+-'
 [/CODE] The two methods I've tried produced errors. New-style formatting runs into the following error (due to the {m,n} usage): [CODE] >>> import config
>>> regex = '([0-9]{1,3}[%])([{0}]?)'.format(config.SERIES)
KeyError: '1,3'
 [/CODE] Old-style formatting has its own problems (due to the '%' character): [CODE] >>> import config
>>> regex = '([0-9]{1,3}[%])([%s]?)' % (config.SERIES)
unsupported format character ']' (0x5d) at index 14
 [/CODE] I haven't been able to get escape characters working inside the regex. Any ideas on how do do this? Thanks, Mike
answer:
You can use [CODE] %% [/CODE] to insert a percent-sign using the old-style formatting: [CODE] '([0-9]{1,3}[%%])([%s]?)' % (config.SERIES)
 [/CODE] Similarly for the new-style formatting, double the braces: [CODE] '([0-9]{{1,3}}[%])([{0}]?)'.format(config.SERIES)
 [/CODE]

title: Purpose of __init__
question:
Purpose of __init__ I've done some reading and can't grasp this as fully as I'd like to. I'm making a little "choose your own adventure" game from the LPTHW tutorial, here's the full script: http://codepad.org/YWVUlHnU What I don't understand is the following: [CODE] class Game(object):

    def __init__(self, start):
        self.quips = [
            "You died. Please try again.",
            "You lost, better luck next time.",
            "Things didn't work out well. You'll need to start over."
            "You might need to improve your skills. Try again." 
        ]
        self.start = start
 [/CODE] I get that we're creating a class, but why define [CODE] __init__ [/CODE] ? Later on I do stuff like [CODE] print self.quis[randint(0, len(self.quips)-1)] [/CODE] which prints one of the four strings in [CODE] quips [/CODE] , but why wouldn't I just create a function called [CODE] quips [/CODE] or something?
answer:
When you call [CODE] Game("central_corridor") [/CODE] , a new object is created and the [CODE] Game.__init__() [/CODE] method is called with that new object as the first argument ( [CODE] self [/CODE] ) and [CODE] "central_corridor" [/CODE] as the second argument. Since you wrote [CODE] a_game = Game(...) [/CODE] , you have assigned [CODE] a_game [/CODE] to refer to that new object. This graphic may make the process easier to understand: Note: The [CODE] __new__ [/CODE] method is provided by Python. It creates a new object of the class given as the first argument. The built-in [CODE] __new__ [/CODE] method doesn't do anything with the remaining arguments. If you need to, you can override the [CODE] __new__ [/CODE] method and utilize the other arguments. The practical reason [CODE] __init__() [/CODE] exists in your program is set the [CODE] start [/CODE] attribute on the [CODE] Game [/CODE] instance you create (the one you call [CODE] a_game [/CODE] ), so that the first call to [CODE] a_game.play() [/CODE] starts in the location where you want it to. You're right about [CODE] quips [/CODE] . There is no reason to have [CODE] quips [/CODE] be set up in [CODE] __init__() [/CODE] . You can just make it a class attribute: [CODE] class Game(object):
    quips = ["You died. Please try again.",
            "You lost, better luck next time.",
            "Things didn't work out well. You'll need to start over."
            "You might need to improve your skills. Try again." ]
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.start = start
 [/CODE]

title: Is it common/good practice to test for type values in Python?
answer: Nope, in fact it's overwhelmingly common not to test for type values, as in your second approach. The idea is that a client of your code (i.e. some other programmer who uses your class) should be able to pass any kind of object that has all the appropriate methods or properties. If it doesn't happen to be an instance of some particular class, that's fine; your code never needs to know the difference. This is called duck typing , because of the adage "If it quacks like a duck and flies like a duck, it might as well be a duck" (well, that's not the actual adage but I got the gist of it I think) One place you'll see this a lot is in the standard library, with any functions that handle file input or output. Instead of requiring an actual [CODE] file [/CODE] object, they'll take anything that implements the [CODE] read() [/CODE] or [CODE] readline() [/CODE] method (depending on the function), or [CODE] write() [/CODE] for writing. In fact you'll often see this in the documentation, e.g. with [CODE] tokenize.generate_tokens [/CODE] , which I just happened to be looking at earlier today: The [CODE] generate_tokens() [/CODE] generator requires one argument, readline , which must be a callable object which provides the same interface as the [CODE] readline() [/CODE] method of built-in file objects (see section File Objects ). Each call to the function should return one line of input as a string. This allows you to use a [CODE] StringIO [/CODE] object (like an in-memory file), or something wackier like a dialog box, in place of a real file. In your own code, just access whatever properties of an object you need, and if it's the wrong kind of object, one of the properties you need won't be there and it'll throw an exception.

title: Calling flask restful API resource methods
question:
Calling flask restful API resource methods I'm creating an API with Flask that is being used for a mobile platform, but I also want the application itself to digest the API in order to render web content. I'm wondering what the best way is to access API resource methods inside of Flask? For instance if I have the following class added as a resource: [CODE] class FooAPI(Resource):
    def __init__(self):
        # Do some things
        super(FooAPI, self).__init__()
    def post(self, id):
        #return something
    def get(self):
        #return something

api = Api(app)
api.add_resource(FooAPI, '/api/foo', endpoint = 'foo')
 [/CODE] Then in a controller I want: [CODE] @app.route("/bar")
def bar():
   #Get return value from post() in FooAPI
 [/CODE] How do I get the return value of post() from FooAPI? Can I do it somehow through the api variable? Or do I have to create an instance of FooAPI in the controller? It seems like there has to be an easy way to do this that I'm just not understanding...
answer: The obvious way for your application to consume the API is to invoke it like any other client.  The fact that the application would be acting as a server and a client at the same time does not matter, the client portion can place requests into [CODE] localhost [/CODE] and the server part will get them in the same way it gets external requests. To generate HTTP requests you can use requests , or urllib2 from the standard library. But while the above method will work just fine it seems overkill to me. In my opinion a better approach is to expose the common functionality of your application in a way that both the regular application and the API can invoke. For example, you could have a package called [CODE] FooLib [/CODE] that implements all the shared logic, then [CODE] FooAPI [/CODE] becomes a thin wrapper around [CODE] FooLib [/CODE] , and both [CODE] FooAPI [/CODE] and [CODE] FooApp [/CODE] call [CODE] FooLib [/CODE] to get things done.

title: Reading a line from standard input in Python
question: Reading a line from standard input in Python What (if any) are the differences between the following two methods of reading a line from standard input: [CODE] raw_input() [/CODE] and [CODE] sys.stdin.readline() [/CODE] ? And in which cases one of these methods is preferable over the other ?
answer: raw_input() takes an optional [CODE] prompt [/CODE] argument. It also strips the trailing newline character from the string it returns, and supports history features if the readline module is loaded. readline() takes an optional [CODE] size [/CODE] argument, does not strip the trailing newline character and does not support history whatsoever. Since they don't do the same thing, they're not really interchangeable. I personally prefer using [CODE] raw_input() [/CODE] to fetch user input, and [CODE] readline() [/CODE] to read lines out of a file.

title: Extract traceback info from an exception object
answer:
The traceback is not stored in the exception. (Not, that is, in Python 2; see Vyktor 's answer for more about the situation in Python 3). Within an [CODE] except [/CODE] clause, you can retrieve it using [CODE] sys.exc_info() [/CODE] . See also the [CODE] traceback [/CODE] module for a few useful tools. [CODE] >>> import sys, traceback
>>> def raise_exception():
...     try:
...         raise Exception
...     except Exception:
...         ex_type, ex, tb = sys.exc_info()
...         traceback.print_tb(tb)
...     finally:
...         del tb
... 
>>> raise_exception()
  File "<stdin>", line 3, in raise_exception
 [/CODE] Or, in your case (since you can't modify the [CODE] try/except [/CODE] block): [CODE] >>> def view_traceback():
...     ex_type, ex, tb = sys.exc_info()
...     traceback.print_tb(tb)
...     del tb
... 
>>> try:
...     raise Exception
... except Exception:
...     view_traceback()
... 
  File "<stdin>", line 2, in <module>
 [/CODE] To elaborate, [CODE] sys.exc_info [/CODE] returns the exception, exception type, and traceback for whatever exception is currently being handled. But as your edit indicates, you're trying to get the traceback that would have been printed if your exception had not been handled, after it has already been handled. That's a much harder question. "Normal" exceptions don't store traceback information, perhaps because keeping exceptions lightweight allows for faster execution when an exception does occur. (Also, as ecatmur observes, storing tracebacks in local variables creates circular references.) And unfortunately, [CODE] sys.exc_info [/CODE] returns [CODE] (None, None, None) [/CODE] when no exception is being handled. Other related [CODE] sys [/CODE] attribues don't help either. [CODE] sys.exc_traceback [/CODE] is deprecated and undefined when no exception is being handled; [CODE] sys.last_traceback [/CODE] seems perfect, but I believe is only defined in interactive sessions. If you can control how the exception is raised, you might be able to use [CODE] inspect [/CODE] and a custom exception to store some of the information. But I'm not even sure how that would work. I'll add that catching and returning an exception is kind of an unusual thing to do; I would suggest refactoring.

title: scipy large sparse matrix
question:
scipy large sparse matrix I'm trying to use large 10^5x10^5 sparse matrices but seem to be running up against scipy: [CODE] n = 10 ** 5
x = scipy.sparse.rand(n, n, .001)
 [/CODE] gets [CODE] ValueError: Trying to generate a random sparse matrix such as the
    product of dimensions is greater than 2147483647 - this is not
    supported on this machine
 [/CODE] Does anyone know why limit is there and if I can avoid it? 
(fyi, I'm using a macbook air with 4gb memory and the enthought distribution)
answer:
This is a limitation which results from the way [CODE] scipy.sparse.rand() [/CODE] is implemented.  You can roll your own random matrix generation to circumvent this limitation: [CODE] n = 10 ** 5
density = 1e-3
ij = numpy.random.randint(n, size=(2, n * n * density))
data = numpy.random.rand(n * n * density)
matrix = scipy.sparse.coo.coo_matrix((data, ij), (n, n))
 [/CODE]

XML parsing - ElementTree vs SAX and DOM
question: XML parsing - ElementTree vs SAX and DOM Python has several ways to parse XML... I understand the very basics of parsing with SAX .  It functions as a stream parser, with an event-driven API. I understand the DOM parser also.  It reads the XML into memory and coverts it to objects that can be accessed with Python. Generally speaking, it was easy to choose between the 2 depending on what you needed to do, memory constraints, performance, etc. (hopefully I'm correct so far). Since Python 2.5, we also have ElementTree . How does this compare to DOM and SAX? Which is it more similar to? Why is it better than the previous parsers?
answer: ElementTree is much easier to use, because it represents an XML tree (basically) as a structure of lists, and attributes are represented as dictionaries. ElementTree needs much less memory for XML trees than DOM (and thus is faster), and the parsing overhead via [CODE] iterparse [/CODE] is comparable to SAX. Additionally, [CODE] iterparse [/CODE] returns partial structures, and you can keep memory usage constant during parsing by discarding the structures as soon as you process them. ElementTree, as in Python 2.5, has only a small feature set compared to full-blown XML libraries, but it's enough for many applications. If you need a validating parser or complete XPath support, lxml is the way to go. For a long time, it used to be quite unstable, but I haven't had any problems with it since 2.1. ElementTree deviates from DOM, where nodes have access to their parent and siblings. Handling actual documents rather than data stores is also a bit cumbersome, because text nodes aren't treated as actual nodes. In the XML snippet [CODE] This is a test [/CODE] The string [CODE] test [/CODE] will be the so-called [CODE] tail [/CODE] of element [CODE] b [/CODE] . In general, I recommend ElementTree as the default for all XML processing with Python, and DOM or SAX as the solutions for specific problems.

Matplotlib: Assign Colors to Lines
question:
Matplotlib: Assign Colors to Lines I am trying to plot a variable number of lines in matplotlib where the X, Y data and colors are stored in numpy arrays, as shown below. Is there a way to pass an array of colors into the plot function, so I don't have to take an extra step to assign a color to each line individually? Should I be translating the RGB color arrays to another color format for this to work, such as HSV or other? [CODE] import numpy as np
X = np.arange(1990, 1994)
Y = [[  1.50615936e+08   5.88252480e+07   2.60363587e+08]
     [  1.53193798e+08   5.91663430e+07   2.63123995e+08]
     [  1.55704596e+08   5.94899260e+07   2.65840188e+08]
     [  1.58175186e+08   5.97843680e+07   2.68559452e+08]]
colors = [(0.99609375, 0.3984375, 0.3984375) (0.796875, 0.0, 0.99609375)
          (0.59765625, 0.99609375, 0.0)]
#current way
ax.plot(X, Y)
[ax.lines[i].set_color(color) for i, color in enumerate(colors)]
#way I feel it can be done, but doesn't work currently
ax.plot(X, Y, color=colors)
plt.show()
 [/CODE] Any help is greatly appreciated.
answer:
I think you want to use the [CODE] Axes [/CODE] method [CODE] set_color_cycle [/CODE] . As you can imagine, it sets the list of colors that are cycled through when colors are assigned by default, i.e. when no color keyword is provided to the [CODE] plot [/CODE] call. Here's an extended version of your example: [CODE] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

X = np.arange(1990, 1994)
Y = [[  1.50615936e+08,   5.88252480e+07,   2.60363587e+08],
     [  1.53193798e+08,   5.91663430e+07,   2.63123995e+08],
     [  1.55704596e+08,   5.94899260e+07,   2.65840188e+08],
     [  1.58175186e+08,   5.97843680e+07,   2.68559452e+08]]
colors = [(0.99609375, 0.3984375, 0.3984375), 
          (0.796875, 0.0, 0.99609375),
          (0.59765625, 0.99609375, 0.0)]

fig = plt.figure()
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(211)
ax1.set_title('old way')
ax1.plot(X, Y)
[ax1.lines[i].set_color(color) for i, color in enumerate(colors)]

ax2 = fig.add_subplot(212)
ax2.set_title('new way')
ax2.set_color_cycle(colors)
ax2.plot(X, Y)

fig.savefig('manycolors.py')
plt.show()
 [/CODE] This results in two subplots with the identically colored lines:

Using property() on classmethods
question:
Using property() on classmethods I have a class with two class methods (using the classmethod() function) for getting and setting what is essentially a static variable.  I tried to use the property() function with these, but it results in an error.  I was able to reproduce the error with the following in the interpreter: [CODE] >>> class foo(object):
...     _var=5
...     def getvar(cls):
...             return cls._var
...     getvar=classmethod(getvar)
...     def setvar(cls,value):
...             cls._var=value
...     setvar=classmethod(setvar)
...     var=property(getvar,setvar)
...
>>> f.getvar()
5
>>> f.setvar(4)
>>> f.getvar()
4
>>> f.var
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in ?
TypeError: 'classmethod' object is not callable
>>> f.var=5
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in ?
TypeError: 'classmethod' object is not callable
 [/CODE] Is it possible to use the property() function with classmethod decorated functions?
answer:
Reading the Python 2.2 release notes, I find the following. The get method [of a property] won't be called when
  the property is accessed as a class
  attribute (C.x) instead of as an
  instance attribute (C().x). If you
  want to override the __get__ operation
  for properties when used as a class
  attribute, you can subclass property -
  it is a new-style type itself - to
  extend its __get__ method, or you can
  define a descriptor type from scratch
  by creating a new-style class that
  defines __get__, __set__ and
  __delete__ methods. NOTE: The below method doesn't actually work for setters, only getters. Therefore, I believe the prescribed solution is to create a ClassProperty as a subclass of property. [CODE] class ClassProperty(property):
    def __get__(self, cls, owner):
        return self.fget.__get__(None, owner)()

class foo(object):
    _var=5
    def getvar(cls):
        return cls._var
    getvar=classmethod(getvar)
    def setvar(cls,value):
        cls._var=value
    setvar=classmethod(setvar)
    var=ClassProperty(getvar,setvar)

assert foo.getvar() == 5
foo.setvar(4)
assert foo.getvar() == 4
assert foo.var == 4
foo.var = 3
assert foo.var == 3
 [/CODE] However, the setters don't actually work: [CODE] foo.var = 4
assert foo.var == foo._var # raises AssertionError
 [/CODE] [CODE] foo._var [/CODE] is unchanged, you've simply overwritten the property with a new value. You can also use [CODE] ClassProperty [/CODE] as a decorator: [CODE] class Foo(object):
    _var = 5

    @ClassProperty
    @classmethod
    def var(cls):
        return cls._var

    @var.setter
    @classmethod
    def var(cls, value):
        cls._var = value

assert foo.var == 5
 [/CODE]

Using django-filter to filter by a single date I am trying to filter time ranges (like [CODE] '2014-12-27' < time <= '2014-12-28' [/CODE] ) using only one parameter. I currently use a url like this for getting a single day [CODE] http://127.0.0.1:8000/movieapi/movieshowtime/?mixtime=2014-12-27&maxtime=2014-12-28
 [/CODE] I would like to be able to do something like this [CODE] http://127.0.0.1:8000/movieapi/movieshowtime/?timerange=2014-12-27 
 [/CODE] But it does not work. The filterset that I am currently using is [CODE] class MovieShowtimeFilter(django_filters.FilterSet):
    mixtime = django_filters.DateTimeFilter(name="movietime",lookup_type='gte')
    maxtime = django_filters.DateTimeFilter(name="movietime",lookup_type='lt')
    timerange = django_filters.DateRangeFilter(name='movietime')

    class Meta:
        model = MovieShowtime
        fields = ['mixtime','maxtime','timerange']
 [/CODE]

Answer: The [CODE] DateRangeFilter [/CODE] provided by [CODE] django-filter [/CODE] allows you to filter across common date ranges like "today", "the past week", "last month", etc. It does not allow you to filter a queryset down to a specific date. You should be able to do this with a custom filter though. [CODE] from django_filters.filters import DateFilter

class WithinDateFilter(DateFilter):

    def filter(self, qs, value):
        from datetime import timedelta

        if value:
            date_value = value.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0)

            filter_lookups = {
                "%s__range" % (self.name, ): (
                    value,
                    value + timedelta(days=1),
                ),
            }

            qs = qs.filter(**filter_lookups)

        return qs
 [/CODE] This should allow you to pass in the single date through the url, and have the query be filtered to only times within that specific date. [CODE] class MovieShowtimeFilter(django_filters.FilterSet):
    timerange = WithinDateFilter(name='movietime')

    class Meta:
        model = MovieShowtime
        fields = ['mixtime','maxtime','timerange']
 [/CODE]

title: Matplotlib mixed subplots with plot and pcolor(mesh) to have the same x axis length when colorbar is on
question: Matplotlib mixed subplots with plot and pcolor(mesh) to have the same x axis length when colorbar is on I am wondering if it is possible to have a subplot with a mixture of graphs drawn with plot() and figures drawn with pcolormesh() that would have the same x axis length. I attached 2 images one when the pcolormesh() subplot does not have the colorbar drawn when the x axes are the same length and one that has the colorbar when the pcolormesh() subplot is shrunk so that it accommodates the colorbar. I would like to have the colorbar, but it should be extending the length of the whole plot and not shrink the subplot. Is this possible without sub-classing any of the current classes?
answer:
Sure, it's possible! What's happening is that a new axes is being created for the colorbar, and the space is being taken from the axes that [CODE] pcolormesh [/CODE] is plotted in.  If you don't want this to happen, you can specify an axes object for the colorbar to go in.  Alternately, you could just use a horizontal colorbar. At any rate, let's reproduce your problem with stand-alone data: [CODE] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1977)

# Generate some interesting-looking random data...
num = 200
grid = np.random.normal(0, 1, (20, num)).cumsum(axis=1).cumsum(axis=0)
x = np.linspace(0, 360, num)
y1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()
y2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()

# Plot on three seperate axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=3, sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(x, y1)
axes[1].plot(x, y2)
im = axes[2].imshow(grid, extent=[0, 360, 0, 20], aspect='auto')
fig.colorbar(im)

plt.show()
 [/CODE] A quick fix is to just use a horizontal colorbar: [CODE] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1977)

# Generate some interesting-looking random data...
num = 200
grid = np.random.normal(0, 1, (20, num)).cumsum(axis=1).cumsum(axis=0)
x = np.linspace(0, 360, num)
y1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()
y2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()

# Plot on three seperate axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=3, sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(x, y1)
axes[1].plot(x, y2)
im = axes[2].imshow(grid, extent=[0, 360, 0, 20], aspect='auto')
fig.colorbar(im, orientation='horizontal')

plt.show()
 [/CODE] Alternately, you can manually add another axes for the colorbar.  We'll also adjust things a bit to make more room. (Side note: Don't use [CODE] tight_layout [/CODE] after making the extra axes. We're no longer working with a nice grid of subplots once we add the additional one, so [CODE] tight_layout [/CODE] will not work correctly.  It's safe to use it before, though you may want to modify the call to [CODE] subplots_adjust [/CODE] in that case.) [CODE] import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1977)

# Generate some interesting-looking random data...
num = 200
grid = np.random.normal(0, 1, (20, num)).cumsum(axis=1).cumsum(axis=0)
x = np.linspace(0, 360, num)
y1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()
y2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, num).cumsum()

# Plot on three seperate axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=3, sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(x, y1)
axes[1].plot(x, y2)
im = axes[2].imshow(grid, extent=[0, 360, 0, 20], aspect='auto')

# Make some room for the colorbar
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.07, right=0.87)

# Add the colorbar outside...
box = axes[2].get_position()
pad, width = 0.02, 0.02
cax = fig.add_axes([box.xmax + pad, box.ymin, width, box.height])
fig.colorbar(im, cax=cax)

plt.show()
 [/CODE]

title: Get consecutive capitalized words using regex
question:
Get consecutive capitalized words using regex I am having trouble with my regex for capturing consecutive capitalized words.
Here is what I want the regex to capture: [CODE] "said Polly Pocket and the toys" -> Polly Pocket
 [/CODE] Here is the regex I am using: [CODE] re.findall('said ([A-Z][\w-]*(\s+[A-Z][\w-]*)+)', article)
 [/CODE] It returns the following: [CODE] [('Polly Pocket', ' Pocket')]
 [/CODE] I want it to return: [CODE] ['Polly Pocket']
 [/CODE]
answer:
Use a positive look-ahead: [CODE] ([A-Z][a-z]+(?=\s[A-Z])(?:\s[A-Z][a-z]+)+)
 [/CODE] Assert that the current word, to be accepted, needs to be followed by another word with a capital letter in it. Broken down: [CODE] (                # begin capture
  [A-Z]            # one uppercase letter  \ First Word
  [a-z]+           # 1+ lowercase letters  /
  (?=\s[A-Z])      # must have a space and uppercase letter following it
  (?:                # non-capturing group
    \s               # space
    [A-Z]            # uppercase letter   \ Additional Word(s)
    [a-z]+           # lowercase letter   /
  )+              # group can be repeated (more words)
)               #end capture
 [/CODE]

Answer: You could estimate (or use a mono width font) to achieve this. Let's assume data is a nested array like [['a1','a2'],['b1','b2']] We can get the max characters in each column. The set the width to that. Width is exactly the width of a monospace font (well not changing other styles at least). Even if you use a variable width font it is a decent estimation. for row in data:
    for i, cell in enumerate(row):
        if len(column_widths) > i:
            if len(cell) > column_widths[i]:
                column_widths[i] = len(cell)
        else:
            column_widths += [len(cell)]

for i, column_width in enumerate(column_widths):
    worksheet.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(i+1)].width = column_width
 [/CODE] A bit of a hack but your reports will be more readable.

title: salt-stack : adding grains to minion or to top file
answer:
You can't create a grain in the top file. Can you point me to the documentation that's telling you that? All a top file does is define which Salt states (sls files) should be applied to which servers. You can use grains to match in your top file. You don't declare grains in your top file. You can create a Salt state that will add a grain to your minion for you and reference that in your top file. Docs here: http://docs.saltstack.com/en/latest/ref/states/all/salt.states.grains.html#salt.states.grains.present Here's an example $ cat /srv/salt/top.sls [CODE] base:
  'server01':
    - rolegrain
 [/CODE] $ cat /srv/salt/rolegrain.sls [CODE] role:
  grains.present:
    - value: application_server
 [/CODE] When running a highstate, this would cause your server with the Salt id of [CODE] server01 [/CODE] to have a grain with the key [CODE] role [/CODE] and value [CODE] application_server [/CODE] . That would look like this: [CODE] salt server01 state.highstate
 [/CODE] or [CODE] salt server01 state.sls rolegrain
 [/CODE] Then you'd get this output [CODE] salt server01 grains.item role

server01:
    ----------
    role:
        application_server
 [/CODE] For completeness, here's some docs. The top file: http://docs.saltstack.com/en/latest/ref/states/top.html Grains: http://docs.saltstack.com/en/latest/topics/targeting/grains.html

Answer: You can't create a grain in the top file. Can you point me to the documentation that's telling you that? All a top file does is define which Salt states (sls files) should be applied to which servers. You can use grains to match in your top file. You don't declare grains in your top file. You can create a Salt state that will add a grain to your minion for you and reference that in your top file. Docs here: http://docs.saltstack.com/en/latest/ref/states/all/salt.states.grains.html#salt.states.grains.present Here's an example $ cat /srv/salt/top.sls [CODE] base:
  'server01':
    - rolegrain
 [/CODE] $ cat /srv/salt/rolegrain.sls [CODE] role:
  grains.present:
    - value: application_server
 [/CODE] When running a highstate, this would cause your server with the Salt id of [CODE] server01 [/CODE] to have a grain with the key [CODE] role [/CODE] and value [CODE] application_server [/CODE] . That would look like this: [CODE] salt server01 state.highstate
 [/CODE] or [CODE] salt server01 state.sls rolegrain
 [/CODE] Then you'd get this output [CODE] salt server01 grains.item role

server01:
    ----------
    role:
        application_server

title: Installing Python 2 and 3 separately
question: Installing Python 2 and 3 separately Is there a way to install python 2 and python 3 on Mac OSX together and be able to switch back and forth? I use Python 2 and 3 for development and I used to be able to do this virtualenv thing where I do source deactivate the development environment. But I wasn't sure how I set that up and it started to get very confusing for the compiler because I apparently installed some modules in one place and it works on python 2 but not 3 (or vice versa) and things are just all over the place. So I am wiping out my whole laptop and this time I want to do this installation business right. Is there any way I can switch back and forth python 2 and 3 with the compiler detecting just one set of library?
answer: Virtualenv is the default answer to that and it's explained well throughout their pages and across the web. An alternative, which does not depend on the shell, is its "reincarnation" as a Python module, pew, the Python Env Wrapper . Both will allow you to have separate interpreters, even for entirely different version numbers.

title: What are sqlite development headers and how to install them?
question: What are sqlite development headers and how to install them? I am trying to install pysqlite and have troubles with that. I found out that the most probable reason of that is missing sqlite headers and I have to install them. However, I have no ideas what these headers are (where I can find them, what they are doing and how to install them). Can anybody, pleas, help me with that?
answer:
debian/ubuntu: [CODE] $ apt-get install libsqlite3-dev # or rpm -i sqlite-devel-something.rpm
 [/CODE] I think a number of interpreters just recompile their small connection libraries on installation, but to do that they need the C .h files in addition to the library to link against. You may already have the library, because something else depended on it, but you don't necessarily have the [CODE] dev [/CODE] package, which is kind of half-way between source and binary. Part of it is straightforward, if you are going to develop with a library you need its interface headers. But I think something more happened, at first, people tried all-source and all-binary distributions, but the all-binary ones were vulnerable to dependency hell , and the all-source ones were overkill. I think now that an interesting compromise is in use, a semi-source distribution where a program links to installed libraries by recompiling those parts of it that link to extension libraries. This makes a lot of sense with interpreters where most of the system can arrive in binary but the extension modules are dynamically loaded and compiled for the installed system. I think.

sqlalchemy dynamic mapping
answer:
It seems that you can just use the attributes directly instead of using the [CODE] columns [/CODE] [CODE] dict [/CODE] . Consider the following setup: [CODE] from sqlalchemy import Table, Column, Integer, Unicode, MetaData, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import mapper, create_session

class Word(object):
    pass

wordColumns = ['english', 'korean', 'romanian']
e = create_engine('sqlite://')
metadata = MetaData(bind=e)

t = Table('words', metadata, Column('id', Integer, primary_key=True),
    *(Column(wordCol, Unicode(255)) for wordCol in wordColumns))
metadata.create_all()
mapper(Word, t)
session = create_session(bind=e, autocommit=False, autoflush=True)
 [/CODE] With that empty class you can do: [CODE] w = Word()
w.english = u'name'
w.korean = u'ì´ë¦'
w.romanian = u'nume'

session.add(w)
session.commit()
 [/CODE] And when you want to access the data: [CODE] w = session.query(Word).filter_by(english=u'name').one()
print w.romanian
 [/CODE] That's the whole [CODE] sqlalchemy [/CODE] 's ORM point , instead of using a [CODE] tuple [/CODE] or [CODE] dict [/CODE] to access the data, you use attribute-like access on your own class. So I was wondering for reasons you'd like to use a [CODE] dict [/CODE] . Perhaps it's because you have strings with the language names. Well, for that you could use python's [CODE] getattr [/CODE] and [CODE] setattr [/CODE] instead, as you would on any python object: [CODE] language = 'korean'
print getattr(w, language)
 [/CODE] That should solve all of your issues. That said, if you still want to use [CODE] dict [/CODE] -like access to the columns, it is also possible. You just have to implement a [CODE] dict [/CODE] -like object. I will now provide code to do this, even though I think it's absolutely unnecessary clutter, since attribute access is so clean. If your issue is already solved by using the method above, don't use the code below this point. You could do it on the [CODE] Word [/CODE] class: [CODE] class Word(object):
    def __getitem__(self, item): 
        return getattr(self, item)
    def __setitem__(self, item, value):
        return setattr(self, item, value)
 [/CODE] The rest of the setup works as above. Then you could use it like this: [CODE] w = Word()
w['english'] = u'name'
 [/CODE] If you want a [CODE] columns [/CODE] attribute then you need a [CODE] dict [/CODE] -like [CODE] class AttributeDict(DictMixin):
    def __init__(self, obj):
        self._obj = obj
    def __getitem__(self, item):
        return getattr(self._obj, item)
    def __setitem__(self, item, value):
        return setattr(self._obj, item, value)

class Word(object):
    def __init__(self):
        self.columns = AttributeDict(self)
 [/CODE] Then you could use as you intended: [CODE] w = Word()
w.columns['english'] = u'name'

title: What's the best way to serialize a large scipy sparse matrix?
question:
What's the best way to serialize a large scipy sparse matrix? I have a large scipy sparse matrix, which is taking up >90% of my total system memory. I would like to save it to disk, as it takes hours to build the matrix... I tried cPickle, but that leads to a major memory explosion... [CODE] import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix
import cPickle

dim = 10**8

M = lil_matrix((dim, dim), dtype=np.float)

with open(filename, 'wb') as f:
    cpickle.dump(M, f)  # leads to a major memory explosion, presumably there is lots of copying
 [/CODE] while HDF5 didn't like the datatype: TypeError: Object dtype dtype('O') has no native HDF5 equivalent So what should I do?
answer: Pickling is very memory inefficient, unfortunately. I would recommend accessing the underlying data array attributes of the sparse matrix, and storing those in an efficient manner, such as hdf5. Reconstructing a sparse matrix from a triplet of row/column/data vectors should be easy.

question:

 [/CODE] to the [CODE] MANIFEST.in [/CODE] file, but when I run [CODE] python setup.py sdist

According to the docs : [CODE] include pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - include all
  files matching any of the listed
  patterns [CODE] exclude pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - exclude all files matching any of the listed patterns [CODE] recursive-include dir pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - include all files
  under dir matching any of the listed
  patterns [CODE] recursive-exclude dir pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - exclude all files under
  dir matching any of the listed
  patterns [CODE] global-include pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - include all files anywhere in
  the source tree matching â & any of
  the listed patterns [CODE] global-exclude pat1 pat2 [/CODE] - exclude
  all files anywhere in the source tree
  matching â & any of the listed
  patterns [CODE] prune dir [/CODE] - exclude
  all files under dir [CODE] graft dir [/CODE] - include all files under dir So seems like you want [CODE] graft [/CODE] , not [CODE] include [/CODE] .
Also, it seems you can't include empty directories. You have to create a " [CODE] empty.txt [/CODE] " file or something like this inside the directory to force its inclusion.

title: clean way to accomplish -- if x in [(0, 1, 2), (2, 0, 1), (1, 2, 0)]:?
question:
clean way to accomplish -- if x in [(0, 1, 2), (2, 0, 1), (1, 2, 0)]:? If not, then a canonical name for a function? 'Cycle' makes sense to me, but that's taken. The example in the header is written for clarity and brevity. Real cases I'm working with have a lot of repetition.
(e.g., I want [1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 1] to "match" [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0]) This type of thing is obscuring my algorithm and filling my code with otherwise useless repetition.
answer:
You can get the cycles of the list with: [CODE] def cycles(a):
    return [ a[i:] + a[:i] for i in range(len(a)) ]
 [/CODE] You can then check if b is a cycle of a with: [CODE] b in cycles(a)
 [/CODE] If the length of the list is long, or if want to make multiple comparison to the same cycles, it may be beneficial (performance wise) to embed the results in a set. [CODE] set_cycles = set(cycles(a))
b in set_cycles
 [/CODE] You can prevent necessarily constructing all the cycles by embedding the equality check in the list and using any: [CODE] any( b == a[i:]+a[:i] for i in range(len(a)))
 [/CODE] You could also achieve this effect by turning the [CODE] cycles [/CODE] function into a generator.

title: axis range in scatter graphs
question:
axis range in scatter graphs I have been using the code below to plot the time spent to run 4 functions. The x axis represents the number of executions whereas the y axis represents the time spent 
running a function. I was wondering if you could help me accomplish the following: 1) set the limits of the x axis so that only positive values are shown (x represents
the number of times each function was executed and is, therefore, always positive) 2) create a legend for the 4 functions Thank you, Mark [CODE] import matplotlib
from matplotlib.backends.backend_agg import FigureCanvasAgg as FigureCanvas
from matplotlib.figure import Figure
import matplotlib.mlab as mlab


r = mlab.csv2rec('performance.csv')

fig = Figure(figsize=(9,6))

canvas = FigureCanvas(fig)

ax = fig.add_subplot(111)

ax.set_title("Function performance",fontsize=14)

ax.set_xlabel("code executions",fontsize=12)

ax.set_ylabel("time(s)",fontsize=12)

ax.grid(True,linestyle='-',color='0.75')

ax.scatter(r.run,r.function1,s=10,color='tomato');
ax.scatter(r.run,r.function2,s=10,color='violet');
ax.scatter(r.run,r.function3,s=10,color='blue');
ax.scatter(r.run,r.function4,s=10,color='green');

canvas.print_figure('performance.png',dpi=700)
 [/CODE]
answer:
You need to call [CODE] legend [/CODE] for the legend to appear. The [CODE] label [/CODE] kwarg only sets the [CODE] _label [/CODE] attribute on the artist object in question. It's there for convenience, so that the label in the legend can be clearly associated with the plotting command. It won't add the legend to the plot without explicitly calling [CODE] ax.legend(...) [/CODE] .  Also, you want [CODE] ax.set_xlim [/CODE] , not [CODE] ax.xlim [/CODE] to adjust the xaxis limits. Have a look at [CODE] ax.axis [/CODE] as well. It sounds like you want something like this: [CODE] import matplotlib as mpl
mpl.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Generate some data
x = np.arange(0, 22, 2)
f1, f2, f3, f4 = np.cumsum(np.random.random((4, x.size)) - 0.5, axis=1)

# It's much more convenient to just use pyplot's factory functions...
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.set_title("Function performance",fontsize=14)
ax.set_xlabel("code executions",fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("time(s)",fontsize=12)
ax.grid(True,linestyle='-',color='0.75')

colors = ['tomato', 'violet', 'blue', 'green']
labels = ['Thing One', 'Thing Two', 'Thing Three', 'Thing Four']
for func, color, label in zip([f1, f2, f3, f4], colors, labels):
    ax.plot(x, func, 'o', color=color, markersize=10, label=label)

ax.legend(numpoints=1, loc='upper left')
ax.set_xlim([0, x.max() + 1])

fig.savefig('performance.png', dpi=100)
 [/CODE]

title: Python 3 asyncio - yield from vs asyncio.async stack usage
question:
Python 3 asyncio - yield from vs asyncio.async stack usage I'm evaluating different patterns for periodic execution (actual sleep/delays ommited for brevity) using the Python 3 asyncio framework, and I have two pieces of code that behave diffrently and I can't explain why. The first version, which uses [CODE] yield from [/CODE] to call itself recursively exhausts the stack in about 1000 iterations, as I expected. The second version calls the coroutine recursively, but delegates actual event loop execution to [CODE] asyncio.async [/CODE] and doesn't exhaust the stack. Can you explain in detail why the stack isn't being used by the second version? What are the differences between the two ways of executing this coroutine? First version (yield from): [CODE] @asyncio.coroutine
def call_self(self, i):
    print('calling self', i)
    yield from self.call_self(i + 1)
 [/CODE] Second version (asyncio.async): [CODE] @asyncio.coroutine
def call_self(self, i):
    print('calling self', i)
    asyncio.async(self.call_self(i + 1))
 [/CODE]
answer:
The first example, using [CODE] yield from [/CODE] , actually blocks each instance of [CODE] call_self [/CODE] until its recursive call to [CODE] call_self [/CODE] returns. This means the call stack keeps growing until you run out of stack space. As you mentioned, this is the obvious behavior. The second example, using [CODE] asyncio.async [/CODE] , doesn't block anywhere. So, each instance of [CODE] call_self [/CODE] immediately exits after running [CODE] asyncio.async(...) [/CODE] , which means the stack doesn't grow infinitely, which means you don't exhaust the stack. Instead, [CODE] asyncio.async [/CODE] schedules [CODE] call_self [/CODE] gets to be executed on the iteration of the event loop, by wrapping it in a [CODE] asyncio.Task [/CODE] . Here's the [CODE] __init__ [/CODE] for [CODE] Task [/CODE] : [CODE] def __init__(self, coro, *, loop=None):
    assert iscoroutine(coro), repr(coro)  # Not a coroutine function!
    super().__init__(loop=loop)
    self._coro = iter(coro)  # Use the iterator just in case.
    self._fut_waiter = None
    self._must_cancel = False
    self._loop.call_soon(self._step)  # This schedules the coroutine to be run
    self.__class__._all_tasks.add(self)
 [/CODE] The call to [CODE] self._loop.call_soon(self._step) [/CODE] is what actually makes the coroutine execute. Because it's happening in a non-blocking way, the call stack from [CODE] call_self [/CODE] never grows beyond the call to the [CODE] Task [/CODE] constructor. Then the next instance of [CODE] call_self [/CODE] gets kicked off by the event loop on its next iteration (which starts as soon as the previous [CODE] call_self [/CODE] returns, assuming nothing else is running in the event loop), completely outside of the context of the previous [CODE] call_self [/CODE] instance.
